summary: How the thymus forms from the third pharyngeal pouch, fills with T cell precursors, sinks into the anterior mediastinum, and shrinks after puberty. Exam questions link the pouch origin to DiGeorge syndrome and ask you to sort out anterior mediastinal masses.

points: The thymic epithelium comes from endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch (its ventral part).
The dorsal part of the same pouch forms the inferior parathyroid glands, so thymus and inferior parathyroids share an origin.
The fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroids.
Neural crest derived mesenchyme forms the thymic capsule, the septa that divide it into lobules, and the connective tissue around its vessels.
The thymic primordia leave the pharynx, fuse in the midline, and descend into the anterior mediastinum, pulling the inferior parathyroids down below the superior ones.
notes.why: The pharyngeal pouches are endodermal outpockets, and organs that come from the same pouch share an origin and often a fate. Because the thymus and the inferior parathyroids both come from the third pouch, the descending thymus pulls the inferior parathyroids down past the glands from the fourth pouch, which is why the inferior glands come from the higher pouch. Neural crest cells supply the mesenchyme around the thymic epithelium, so a neural crest defect can impair the thymus even when the endoderm is normal. Parathyroid tissue that fails to separate can end up anywhere along this path, including inside the thymus.

notes.h: Filling the thymus with T cells
points: The endoderm forms a meshwork of epithelial reticular cells; it does not make lymphocytes itself.
T cell precursors made in fetal liver and bone marrow travel in the blood and colonize this framework during fetal life.
The lobules then split into a dense outer cortex of immature thymocytes and a paler inner medulla.
Hassall corpuscles, whorls of keratinizing epithelial reticular cells, appear in the medulla.
notes.why: The thymus is a stromal organ: its epithelial reticular cells supply the signals (such as Notch ligands and IL-7) and the self peptides on MHC that guide T cell maturation, while the lymphocytes themselves are immigrants from blood-forming sites. Precursors enter near the corticomedullary junction, move out to the cortex as they multiply, and then move inward to the medulla as they mature. That traffic explains why the cortex is crowded and dark while the medulla is paler, and Hassall corpuscles mark the medulla on a section.

points: The third and fourth pouches fail to develop, so the thymus and parathyroids are small or absent.
No thymus gives an absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray and a low T cell count, with viral, fungal, and Pneumocystis infections.
No parathyroids gives low PTH and hypocalcemia, which shows up as tetany or seizures in the newborn.
Neural crest cells also fail to build the outflow tract, so conotruncal defects occur: truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch.
Other features: cleft palate and a typical facial appearance.
notes.why: The 22q11.2 microdeletion removes genes including TBX1, which the pharyngeal pouches and arches need to develop normally, including the tissue that neural crest cells populate. Because the third and fourth pouches and the cardiac outflow tract all depend on this tissue, one deletion explains the thymic, parathyroid, and conotruncal defects together. Missing thymic education causes the T cell deficiency, and missing PTH causes hypocalcemia, so a newborn often presents with tetany before infections appear. Most patients keep some thymic tissue, so the T cell defect is usually partial.

points: The thymus is largest relative to body size at birth and reaches its largest absolute size around puberty.
After puberty the cortex shrinks and adipose tissue replaces most of the lymphoid tissue (involution).
Long-lived naive and memory T cells already in the blood and nodes keep dividing on their own, so immunity persists after involution or adult thymectomy.
The adult thymus sits in the anterior and superior mediastinum, behind the manubrium and in front of the great vessels and pericardium.
notes.why: Thymic output of new naive T cells falls after puberty as thymic epithelium declines, partly under the influence of sex steroids, so the cortex thins and fat fills the gland. Naive and memory T cells already in the periphery are long-lived and keep their numbers up by slow homeostatic division driven by IL-7 and contact with self MHC (memory CD8 cells also use IL-15). This is why adult thymectomy, as done for myasthenia gravis, does not cause clinical immunodeficiency, while a congenitally absent thymus does.

points: Thymoma: an epithelial tumor of the thymus in adults, linked to myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, and hypogammaglobulinemia.
Teratoma: a germ cell tumor that may contain fat, calcification, or teeth.
Lymphoma: often Hodgkin (nodular sclerosis) in young adults, with fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.
Retrosternal thyroid: a goiter that extends down from the neck behind the sternum.
notes.why: The anterior mediastinum holds the thymus, lymph nodes, tissue that can extend from the thyroid, and germ cells thought to have strayed during their migration, which explains the classic list of masses there. Thymoma is linked to autoimmunity because the tumor epithelium is thought to select T cells abnormally, letting autoreactive clones escape deletion and drive antibodies against targets such as the acetylcholine receptor. The tissue of origin predicts the clues: fat and calcium in teratoma, B symptoms in lymphoma, and continuity with a neck mass in a retrosternal goiter.

summary: The microscopic layout of lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, and mucosal lymphoid tissue, and which zone holds B cells or T cells. Exam questions ask which zone is empty in an immunodeficiency, which zone grows in a reactive node, and how blood moves through the spleen.

points: Lymph enters through afferent vessels into the subcapsular sinus, then flows through cortical and medullary sinuses to the efferent vessel at the hilum.
Outer cortex: B cell follicles. Primary follicles are resting; secondary follicles have a pale germinal center surrounded by a mantle zone.
Paracortex (deep cortex): T cells and dendritic cells, plus high endothelial venules (HEVs) where naive lymphocytes leave the blood.
Medulla: medullary cords packed with plasma cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes, alternating with medullary sinuses lined by macrophages.
notes.why: A lymph node is a filter where lymph moves slowly from the subcapsular sinus through the cortical and medullary sinuses, past macrophages and dendritic cells that capture antigen. Naive lymphocytes enter from the blood through high endothelial venules in the paracortex, where the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 (acting on CCR7) hold T cells near dendritic cells, and CXCL13 draws B cells on into the follicles. This layout lets dendritic cells present antigen to T cells in the paracortex, lets activated helper T cells meet B cells at the follicle edge, and sends the resulting plasma cells to the medullary cords.

points: DiGeorge syndrome (no T cells): the paracortex is thin or empty, while follicles can still form.
X-linked agammaglobulinemia (no mature B cells): follicles and germinal centers are absent, and tonsils are tiny.
Reactive follicular hyperplasia: large germinal centers from strong B cell stimulation, as in rheumatoid arthritis and early HIV infection.
Reactive paracortical hyperplasia: expanded T cell zone in viral infections such as infectious mononucleosis, after some vaccines, and with drugs such as phenytoin.
notes.why: Each zone is filled by the cell type that homes to it, so a missing lineage leaves its own zone empty while the other zones still form. In DiGeorge syndrome few T cells leave the thymus, so the paracortex is depleted, while in X-linked agammaglobulinemia a BTK defect stops B cells at the pre-B stage, so follicles and germinal centers never form. Reactive patterns follow the same logic in reverse: antigens that drive B cell responses enlarge germinal centers, and viral or drug stimuli that drive T cell proliferation expand the paracortex.

points: White pulp: the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) of T cells wraps the central arteriole; B cell follicles sit beside it.
The marginal zone, between white and red pulp, has macrophages and marginal zone B cells that trap blood-borne antigens and respond to encapsulated bacteria.
Red pulp: splenic cords (cords of Billroth) of macrophages and reticular fibers, and venous sinusoids.
Blood path: splenic artery, trabecular arteries, central arterioles in white pulp, penicillar arterioles, then into cords or sinusoids, then pulp veins, trabecular veins, splenic vein.
Red cells in the cords must squeeze through slits between sinusoid endothelial cells; old or rigid cells get stuck and are eaten by macrophages.
notes.why: The spleen filters blood rather than lymph, so its lymphoid tissue is organized around arterioles instead of sinuses. Much of the arterial blood is released first into the marginal zone, where macrophages and marginal zone B cells capture blood-borne antigens; this is the main defense against encapsulated bacteria, which is why asplenia predisposes to overwhelming pneumococcal, Haemophilus, and meningococcal sepsis. In the red pulp, red cells must deform to pass through narrow endothelial slits, so spherocytes, sickled cells, and cells with inclusions are trapped and removed, and Howell-Jolly bodies appear after splenectomy.

points: Cortex: dark-staining, densely packed immature thymocytes on a network of epithelial reticular cells; positive selection happens here.
The blood thymus barrier in the cortex (continuous endothelium, thick basal lamina, epithelial reticular cell sheath) keeps blood antigens away from developing cells.
Medulla: paler, fewer and more mature T cells, and Hassall corpuscles; negative selection happens here.
The thymus has no lymphoid follicles and no afferent lymphatics, which helps tell it apart from a lymph node.
notes.why: Positive selection in the cortex keeps thymocytes whose receptors bind self MHC on cortical epithelial cells weakly, and this step also decides whether a cell becomes CD4 (class II) or CD8 (class I). Negative selection, mainly in the medulla, deletes cells that bind self peptide strongly, aided by AIRE, which lets medullary epithelial cells express proteins normally found only in other tissues. The blood thymus barrier keeps circulating antigens away from cortical thymocytes during selection. The thymus is an epithelial organ that makes T cells rather than filtering lymph, so it has no afferent lymphatics and no follicles.

points: Includes the palatine, pharyngeal, and lingual tonsils, Peyer patches, and scattered lymphoid nodules along the gut and airways.
Peyer patches are clusters of follicles in the ileal mucosa and submucosa, under a dome of follicle-associated epithelium.
M cells in that epithelium take up antigens from the lumen and pass them to dendritic cells and lymphocytes below.
B cells activated here switch to IgA (TGF-beta drives the switch) and home as plasma cells to the lamina propria.
Plasma cells secrete dimeric IgA joined by a J chain; the polymeric Ig receptor carries it across the epithelium and leaves secretory component attached.
notes.why: Mucosal lymphoid tissue samples antigen straight from the lumen instead of waiting for it to arrive in lymph. M cells carry antigen across the epithelium by transcytosis to dendritic cells in the dome, which prime local T and B cells; TGF-beta and other local signals favor switching to IgA, and the activated cells gain gut-homing receptors so they return to the lamina propria as plasma cells. The polymeric Ig receptor binds dimeric IgA on the basolateral side, carries it through the epithelial cell, and is cleaved at the apical side, leaving secretory component that protects IgA from digestion.

summary: The structure of MHC (HLA) class I and class II molecules, how each one loads peptides, how HLA genes are inherited, and which HLA types are tied to which diseases. Exams also use MHC to explain NK cell killing and why transplant patients need crossmatching.

points: Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C): one heavy (alpha) chain paired with beta2-microglobulin, on all nucleated cells and platelets, not on mature red cells.
Class I shows peptides from inside the cell (8 to 10 amino acids) to CD8 T cells; CD8 binds the alpha3 domain.
Class II (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR): an alpha and a beta chain, on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) and thymic epithelium.
Class II shows peptides from outside the cell (about 13 to 25 amino acids) to CD4 T cells; CD4 binds the beta2 domain.
IFN-gamma increases expression of both classes.
notes.why: The two classes sample different compartments so the right T cell responds. Class I reports on proteins made inside the cell, which signals infection or transformation that CD8 cells must kill, while class II reports on material taken up from outside, which CD4 cells answer by directing help. The class I groove is closed at both ends, limiting peptides to about 8 to 10 residues, while the open class II groove holds longer peptides. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors that bind conserved regions of MHC, which is why CD4 cells are restricted to class II and CD8 cells to class I.

points: Class I path: cytosolic proteins (including viral proteins) are tagged with ubiquitin and cut in the proteasome.
TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing) pumps the peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, where they load onto class I and go to the surface.
Class II path: class II is made in the ER with the invariant chain blocking its groove and steering it to endosomes.
Engulfed proteins are degraded in acidic endosomes; the invariant chain is cut down to a small piece called CLIP.
HLA-DM swaps CLIP out for a foreign peptide, and the loaded class II goes to the surface.
Dendritic cells can also load engulfed antigens onto class I (cross-presentation) to prime CD8 T cells against viruses and tumors.
notes.why: The two pathways keep peptides from the wrong source off each molecule. Class I loads in the ER, where TAP delivers cytosolic peptides, so a TAP defect leaves class I empty and unstable, lowers its surface level, and weakens CD8 responses. Class II is also made in the ER, but the invariant chain blocks its groove until it reaches acidic endosomes, so it cannot pick up cytosolic peptides; HLA-DM then exchanges CLIP for an engulfed peptide. Cross-presentation by dendritic cells bypasses this split so CD8 T cells can be primed against viruses and tumors that do not infect dendritic cells.

points: The HLA genes sit together on the short arm of chromosome 6.
They are highly polymorphic and codominant, so each cell shows the alleles from both parents.
The linked set of HLA genes on one chromosome is a haplotype, and it is usually inherited as a block.
Each child gets one haplotype from each parent, so a sibling has a 25% chance of a full match, 50% chance of a half match, and 25% chance of no match.
A parent and child always share at least one haplotype (at least a half match), barring recombination.
notes.why: The HLA genes are tightly linked, so they travel together as a haplotype, and each parent passes on one of two haplotypes. A sibling matches on both only when each parent happened to pass the same haplotype to both children, a chance of one half times one half, or 25%. Codominant expression of many polymorphic alleles lets each person present a broad range of peptides, which helps a population survive new pathogens but makes unrelated donors unlikely to match. A parent shares at least one haplotype with each child, so a parent is usually a half match.

points: NK cells carry inhibitory receptors (KIRs, CD94/NKG2A) that recognize self class I and turn the NK cell off.
Viruses and tumors often lower class I to escape CD8 T cells, which removes that brake.
If activating signals such as stress ligands are present and class I is missing, the NK cell kills the target.
NK cells also kill antibody-coated cells through CD16 (antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity).
notes.why: NK cell activity is set by the balance of inhibitory and activating signals. Healthy cells display self class I, which engages inhibitory receptors whose cytoplasmic ITIM motifs recruit phosphatases that cancel activating signals. A virus or tumor that lowers class I to escape CD8 T cells removes this brake, and stress ligands such as MICA and MICB (binding NKG2D) supply the activating signal, so the cell is killed. NK cells and CD8 T cells are therefore complementary: escaping one tends to expose the cell to the other.

points: Prior transfusion, pregnancy, or transplant can make a person produce antibodies against foreign HLA (sensitization).
Preformed antibodies against donor HLA or ABO antigens bind graft endothelium and fix complement within minutes to hours (hyperacute rejection).
The graft turns mottled and cyanotic from thrombosis and must be removed; this is type II hypersensitivity.
A crossmatch mixes recipient serum with donor lymphocytes to find these antibodies before surgery.
Closer HLA matching lowers T cell recognition of the graft and improves long-term survival.
notes.why: Sensitizing events expose a person to foreign HLA and leave memory B cells and plasma cells that make antibody against those alleles. When a graft carrying those antigens is perfused, the antibodies bind its endothelium at once and activate complement and platelets, causing thrombosis and ischemic necrosis faster than immunosuppression can prevent. A crossmatch finds these antibodies before surgery. HLA matching acts on a different arm of rejection: fewer mismatched alleles means fewer recipient T cells recognize the graft, which lowers acute and chronic cellular rejection.

summary: Where lymph from each part of the body travels, which palpable node group enlarges with an infection or tumor at a given site, and what happens when the thoracic duct is injured. Exams test this with first-node spread of cancers, the Virchow node, and chylothorax.

points: Lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdomen collects in the cisterna chyli, a sac in front of the L1 to L2 vertebrae just right of the aorta.
The thoracic duct runs up from the cisterna chyli through the aortic hiatus, between the aorta and azygos vein, and crosses to the left at about T4 to T5.
It ends at the left venous angle, where the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins join.
The thoracic duct drains everything except the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right side of the thorax.
That right upper quarter drains through the right lymphatic duct into the right venous angle.
Intestinal lymph (chyle) carries long-chain fat as chylomicrons from the lacteals into the cisterna chyli.
notes.why: Lymph returns leaked interstitial fluid and protein to the venous blood, and the ducts empty where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet on each side. The thoracic duct begins in the abdomen, rises on the right of the midline, and crosses to the left in the posterior mediastinum, so it carries lymph from both lower limbs, the abdomen, and the left upper body, leaving only the right upper quarter for the right lymphatic duct. Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries in the villi, so dietary long-chain fat enters lacteals and reaches the blood through this duct rather than the portal vein.

points: Cervical nodes: scalp, face, mouth, pharynx, and neck.
Supraclavicular nodes: right side drains the mediastinum, lungs, and esophagus; left side receives the thoracic duct and drains the abdomen and thorax.
Axillary nodes: upper limb, most of the breast, and the chest and abdominal wall above the umbilicus.
Epitrochlear nodes: the ulnar (medial) side of the hand and forearm.
Superficial inguinal nodes: skin of the lower limb, abdominal wall below the umbilicus, buttock, perineum, scrotum, vulva, and anal canal below the pectinate line.
Popliteal nodes: the lateral foot and back of the leg, along the small saphenous vein.
notes.why: Lymph from a region drains first to the nearest regional node group, so an enlarged group points back to an infection or tumor in its territory. Superficial lymphatics tend to follow superficial veins, which explains why the epitrochlear node near the basilic vein drains the medial hand and forearm, and the popliteal node near the small saphenous vein drains the lateral foot and back of the leg. Skin and body wall below the umbilicus drain to the superficial inguinal nodes, so a lesion on the leg, buttock, perineum, vulva, or lower anal canal enlarges inguinal nodes.

points: Breast: lateral quadrants drain to axillary nodes (most breast lymph); medial quadrants drain to parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes.
Testis: para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near L1 to L2, following the gonadal vessels back to where the testis formed.
Scrotum: superficial inguinal nodes, because scrotal skin is body wall.
Anal canal above the pectinate line: internal iliac nodes. Below the line: superficial inguinal nodes.
Ovary: para-aortic nodes, the same logic as the testis.
notes.why: Lymphatics from an organ follow its blood vessels, so an organ's first nodes sit where its arteries arise, which can be far from where the organ ends up. The gonads develop on the posterior abdominal wall in the lumbar region and descend, dragging their vessels and lymphatics with them, so testicular and ovarian tumors spread to para-aortic nodes, while scrotal skin is body wall and drains with the perineum to inguinal nodes. The pectinate line marks the junction of endoderm-derived hindgut and ectoderm-derived proctodeum, so lymph drainage, blood supply, and nerve supply all change there.

points: An enlarged, hard left supraclavicular node is the Virchow node.
Tumor cells from the stomach, pancreas, or other abdominal and thoracic organs travel up the thoracic duct and lodge there.
Gastric adenocarcinoma is the classic source; a palpable node there is called the Troisier sign.
notes.why: The thoracic duct empties at the left venous angle, so the left supraclavicular nodes sit at the last station of lymph from the abdomen, pelvis, and much of the thorax. Tumor cells carried up the duct can lodge in or reflux into these nodes, so a hard, fixed left supraclavicular node may be the first sign of a hidden abdominal cancer, classically gastric adenocarcinoma. A hard right supraclavicular node points instead to the mediastinum, lungs, or esophagus, because the right side does not receive abdominal lymph.

points: Injury to the thoracic duct (surgery such as esophagectomy, trauma, or tumor such as lymphoma) leaks chyle into the pleural space.
Pleural fluid is milky white, rich in triglycerides (usually above 110 mg/dL), and contains chylomicrons and many lymphocytes.
Injury below about T5 tends to cause a right chylothorax; injury above that level, after the duct crosses, tends to cause a left one.
Ongoing loss drains fat, protein, fat-soluble vitamins, and lymphocytes.
Medium-chain triglycerides are absorbed straight into portal blood without chylomicrons, so an MCT diet lowers chyle flow.
notes.why: The thoracic duct lies to the right of the midline in the lower posterior mediastinum and crosses to the left at about T4 to T5, so the side of the effusion depends on the level of injury. The duct carries chylomicrons from the gut, so the fluid is milky with a high triglyceride level, and it carries recirculating lymphocytes, so the cells are mostly lymphocytes. A prolonged leak therefore causes malnutrition, fat-soluble vitamin loss, and lymphopenia with impaired immunity. Medium-chain fatty acids enter portal blood directly, so swapping long-chain fat for them reduces flow through the duct.

summary: How antibodies are built and what each isotype does, how B cells get T cell help to switch class, how the T helper subsets differ, and how cytotoxic cells kill. Exams test these with immunodeficiencies, vaccine responses, and antibody titer curves.

points: Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains (kappa or lambda) held together by disulfide bonds.
Fab: the two arms. Variable domains of heavy and light chains each have three hypervariable regions (CDRs) that form the antigen-binding site.
Fc: the stem made of heavy chain constant domains. It sets the isotype and does the work: complement binding (C1q) and Fc receptor binding.
Papain cuts an antibody into two Fab pieces and one Fc piece; pepsin leaves one F(ab')2 piece.
notes.why: An antibody separates recognition from function: the variable Fab arms bind antigen, while the constant Fc stem decides which effector system is engaged. The three CDRs of the heavy and light chains meet at the tip of each arm, and their sequence diversity, generated by V(D)J recombination and later somatic hypermutation, gives each antibody its specificity. Because every antibody of one isotype shares the same Fc, Fc receptors on phagocytes, NK cells, and mast cells, and C1q, can respond to any antibody of that class once it binds antigen. Fab fragments still bind antigen but cannot trigger these effector functions.

points: IgM: pentamer with a J chain, made first in a primary response, best at activating complement; monomer IgM sits on naive B cells.
IgG: monomer, most abundant in serum, crosses the placenta through FcRn, opsonizes, neutralizes, and fixes complement.
IgA: monomer in serum; dimer with J chain and secretory component in tears, saliva, breast milk, and gut secretions.
IgE: binds FcεRI on mast cells and basophils; drives allergy and, with eosinophils, defense against helminths.
IgD: sits with IgM on naive B cells as a receptor; its serum role is unclear.
notes.why: Each isotype is the same variable region joined to a different heavy chain constant region, so the isotype decides where the antibody goes and what it does. IgM is a pentamer with ten binding sites, so it binds with high avidity and engages C1q easily, which suits the early response, and its size keeps it in the blood. IgG is small and binds FcRn, which carries it across the placenta and rescues it from lysosomal breakdown, giving it a half-life of about three weeks. Secretory IgA is built to survive in secretions, and IgE acts while bound to receptors on mast cells rather than free in serum.

notes.h: B cell help and class switching
points: T dependent response: a B cell presents protein peptide on class II to a CD4 helper T cell.
CD40L on the activated T cell binds CD40 on the B cell; cytokines then pick the new isotype (IL-4 to IgE, TGF-beta to IgA, IFN-gamma to opsonizing IgG).
In germinal centers, activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives class switching and somatic hypermutation.
B cells with better-fitting receptors survive, so affinity rises over time (affinity maturation), and memory B cells and plasma cells form.
CD40L defect (X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome): normal or high IgM, very low IgG, IgA, and IgE, with pyogenic and opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis.
T independent response: polysaccharides with repeating units crosslink B cell receptors and give mostly IgM, little memory, and weak responses under age 2.
Conjugate vaccines link polysaccharide to a protein carrier so T cells can help, giving IgG and memory in infants.
notes.why: A B cell binds whole antigen through its receptor, internalizes it, and presents its peptides on class II, so a helper T cell specific for a peptide from the same antigen can help that B cell (linked recognition). CD40 signaling plus cytokines induce AID, which deaminates cytidine in switch regions and variable genes, enabling class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation, and follicular dendritic cells then help select the B cells with the highest affinity. Without CD40L, B cells cannot switch, so patients make only IgM. Polysaccharides cannot be presented on MHC and get no T cell help, which conjugate vaccines fix by attaching the sugar to a protein.

points: Th1: induced by IL-12, makes IFN-gamma, activates macrophages to kill intracellular microbes.
Th2: induced by IL-4, makes IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, drives IgE switching, eosinophils, and mucus.
Th17: induced by IL-6 with TGF-beta (kept up by IL-23), makes IL-17, recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi such as Candida.
Regulatory T cells: CD4, CD25, and FOXP3 positive; secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta to suppress responses. FOXP3 loss causes IPEX syndrome.
notes.why: The cytokines present when a naive CD4 cell is activated set its fate by turning on a master transcription factor: T-bet for Th1, GATA-3 for Th2, ROR-gamma-t for Th17, and FOXP3 for regulatory T cells. Each subset's cytokines reinforce that subset and suppress the others (IFN-gamma inhibits Th2 and IL-4 inhibits Th1), so responses become polarized. The effector cytokines match the threat: IFN-gamma arms macrophages against intracellular microbes, IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 mobilize IgE, eosinophils, and mucus against helminths, and IL-17 recruits neutrophils to mucosal surfaces. Losing FOXP3 removes regulatory cells, so IPEX causes autoimmunity in many organs.

notes.h: How CD8 T cells and NK cells kill
points: Perforin forms pores in the target membrane so granzymes can enter; granzymes activate caspases and trigger apoptosis.
Fas ligand on the killer binds Fas (CD95) on the target and starts the extrinsic apoptosis pathway through caspase-8.
Apoptosis kills without spilling cell contents, so there is little inflammation.
CD8 T cells need foreign peptide on class I; NK cells need no prior exposure and act on cells missing class I.
notes.why: Cytotoxic cells kill by triggering the target cell's own apoptotic machinery. Perforin released into the immune synapse forms pores that let granzyme B into the target, where it activates caspases directly and cleaves BID to engage the mitochondrial pathway. Fas ligand works separately by clustering Fas, which recruits the adaptor FADD and activates caspase-8. Apoptotic cells are packaged and eaten by phagocytes without releasing their contents, so infected cells are removed with little inflammation, unlike necrosis.

points: Primary response: a lag of about a week, IgM first then IgG, low peak titer, low affinity.
Secondary response: shorter lag (a few days), mostly IgG, higher and longer-lasting titer, higher affinity, from memory B cells.
Active immunity: the person's own response after infection or vaccination; slow to start, long-lasting, with memory.
Passive immunity: ready-made antibody such as maternal IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk, or immune globulin; immediate but gone in weeks to months.
Maternal IgG fades by about 6 months, which is when infant infections from encapsulated bacteria rise.
notes.why: In a primary response, rare naive clones must be found, activated, and expanded, and class switching and affinity maturation take time, so the lag is long and IgM comes first. Memory B cells left behind are more numerous, already switched, and of higher affinity, so a second exposure produces mostly IgG faster and in larger amounts. Passive antibody protects at once without activating the recipient's lymphocytes, so no memory forms and the antibody decays with its half-life. Maternal IgG declines over the first months while the infant's own IgG production is still low, leaving a window of vulnerability around 6 months.

tricks.label: Active is earned, passive is borrowed

highYield: A normal or high IgM with low IgG, IgA, and IgE in a boy with Pneumocystis pneumonia points to CD40L deficiency.

Children under 2 respond poorly to plain polysaccharide vaccines, so they get conjugate vaccines.

pitfalls: Fab binds antigen; Fc sets the isotype and binds complement and Fc receptors.
IgA is the most produced antibody overall, but IgG is the most abundant in serum.
Isotype switching changes the heavy chain constant region only; the antigen-binding site stays the same.
Th1 and Th17 both fight bacteria: Th1 helps macrophages with intracellular microbes, Th17 brings neutrophils for extracellular ones.

summary: How innate cells sense microbes and damage, call in leukocytes, start fever and the acute phase response, and eat and kill invaders. Exam questions link each step to a disease: leukocyte adhesion deficiency, Chediak-Higashi syndrome, granulomas, septic shock, and toxic shock syndrome.

points: TLR4 with CD14 (and MD-2) binds LPS (lipid A) from gram-negative bacteria on the cell surface.
TLR5 binds flagellin; TLR2 binds lipoproteins and lipoteichoic acid of gram-positive bacteria.
Endosomal TLRs sense nucleic acids: TLR3 double-stranded RNA, TLR7 and TLR8 single-stranded RNA, TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA.
Most TLRs signal through MyD88 to NF-kappaB, which turns on TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and chemokines; TLR3 and TLR4 also trigger type I interferons.
The NLRP3 inflammasome senses damage signals (DAMPs) such as ATP and urate crystals and activates caspase-1.
Caspase-1 cuts pro-IL-1beta and pro-IL-18 into their active forms; gout flares are driven this way.
notes.why: Innate receptors recognize molecular patterns shared by whole classes of microbes, such as lipid A, flagellin, and unmethylated CpG DNA, which host cells lack or keep out of reach. Their location matches the pattern: surface TLRs detect bacterial wall parts, while nucleic acid sensing TLRs sit in endosomes, where microbial genomes are exposed but host nucleic acids normally do not go. MyD88 signaling activates NF-kappaB, which turns on genes for TNF, IL-6, chemokines, and inactive pro-IL-1beta. The inflammasome supplies a second signal, activating caspase-1 to cleave pro-IL-1beta, which is why urate crystals cause the intense IL-1 driven inflammation of gout.

points: Rolling: endothelial E-selectin and P-selectin bind sialyl Lewis X on leukocytes. P-selectin comes from Weibel-Palade bodies; TNF and IL-1 induce E-selectin.
Tight adhesion: leukocyte integrins (LFA-1 and Mac-1, which share the CD18 chain) bind ICAM-1, which TNF and IL-1 induce on endothelium.
Diapedesis: PECAM-1 (CD31) lets cells squeeze between endothelial cells, mostly in postcapillary venules.
Chemotaxis: C5a, LTB4, IL-8, and bacterial formyl peptides pull neutrophils toward the site.
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (CD18 loss): delayed umbilical cord separation, skin infections without pus, poor wound healing, and a very high blood neutrophil count.
notes.why: Each step uses a different molecular pair, and local mediators switch each one on, so leukocytes leave the blood only at sites of injury. Selectin bonds form and break quickly, which slows leukocytes into rolling; chemokines on the endothelium then shift integrins into a high affinity state, converting rolling into firm adhesion to ICAM-1. In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, CD18 is absent, so neutrophils roll but cannot stick, which keeps them in the blood (a high count) and out of tissue, so infections form no pus and the umbilical stump separates late.

points: IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha act on the hypothalamus, where COX-2 makes PGE2 that raises the temperature set point; NSAIDs block this step.
IL-6 drives the liver to make acute phase proteins.
Rise: CRP (opsonin), fibrinogen (raises ESR), serum amyloid A, ferritin, and hepcidin.
Fall: albumin and transferrin.
Hepcidin blocks ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages, which causes anemia of chronic disease.
Long-standing high serum amyloid A can deposit as AA amyloid.
notes.why: IL-1, IL-6, and TNF act on the hypothalamus, where they induce COX-2 near the preoptic area, and the PGE2 made there raises the temperature set point, so the body conserves and makes heat until core temperature reaches the new set point. IL-6 shifts hepatocyte protein synthesis toward proteins that opsonize, clot, and hold iron, and away from albumin and transferrin, the negative acute phase reactants. Hepcidin causes ferroportin to be internalized and degraded, keeping iron away from microbes, which explains the low serum iron with normal or high ferritin in anemia of chronic disease.

points: Opsonins coat microbes so phagocytes grab them: IgG binds Fc gamma receptors and C3b binds complement receptor 1.
The phagosome fuses with lysosomes (phagolysosome), and microbes are killed by the oxidative burst and lysosomal enzymes.
Chediak-Higashi syndrome: autosomal recessive LYST mutation disrupts lysosome trafficking and phagolysosome fusion.
Findings: giant granules in neutrophils, partial albinism, peripheral neuropathy, recurrent pyogenic infections with S aureus and streptococci, neutropenia, and easy bleeding.
notes.why: Opsonins bridge the microbe and the phagocyte, because phagocytes have receptors for the Fc of IgG and for C3b but bind many bacteria poorly on their own, especially encapsulated ones. After uptake, the phagosome must fuse with lysosomes and granules to deliver its killing enzymes. LYST regulates the size and trafficking of lysosome-related organelles, so its loss produces giant fused granules that deliver their contents poorly, impairing killing. The same organelle defect affects melanosomes, platelet dense granules, and the granules of NK and cytotoxic T cells, which explains the partial albinism, bleeding, and infections.

points: Foreign body granuloma: material too large to engulf (suture, talc, splinter) collects macrophages, epithelioid cells, and foreign body giant cells.
The foreign material is often visible, and talc and many sutures shine under polarized light.
Immune granuloma: macrophages present antigen and make IL-12, Th1 cells make IFN-gamma, and macrophages turn epithelioid and fuse into Langhans giant cells.
TNF keeps immune granulomas intact, so anti-TNF drugs can reactivate latent tuberculosis.
Immune granulomas have a cuff of lymphocytes and may have caseous necrosis (tuberculosis); foreign body granulomas have few T cells.
notes.why: A granuloma walls off something the immune system cannot eliminate. In a foreign body granuloma the stimulus is inert material too large to engulf, so macrophages gather and fuse into giant cells without needing antigen-specific T cells. In an immune granuloma the stimulus is a persistent antigen, often an intracellular microbe such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Th1 cells keep macrophages activated with IFN-gamma while TNF holds the structure together. Blocking TNF loosens the wall and lets contained organisms escape, which is why patients are screened for latent tuberculosis before anti-TNF therapy.

points: In gram-negative sepsis, LPS through TLR4 floods the blood with TNF, IL-1, and IL-6.
Nitric oxide causes vasodilation and hypotension; activated endothelium leaks fluid; tissue factor on monocytes and endothelium starts DIC.
Result: low blood pressure, edema, lactic acidosis, low platelets and fibrinogen, and failing lungs, kidneys, and liver.

SIRS needs two or more: temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F) or below 36 °C (96.8 °F), pulse above 90/min, respirations above 20/min (or PaCO2 below 32 mm Hg), WBC above 12,000/mm3 or below 4,000/mm3 (or more than 10% bands).
Superantigens (S aureus TSST-1, S pyogenes pyrogenic exotoxins) bind MHC class II and the TCR V-beta region outside the peptide groove.
This activates up to about 20% of all T cells at once, releasing IL-2, IFN-gamma, and TNF, which causes fever, diffuse rash with later peeling, and shock.
notes.why: In sepsis a local defense becomes systemic: LPS acting through TLR4 drives release of TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 into the circulation, and effects that help locally become harmful everywhere. Inducible nitric oxide synthase makes nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, causing hypotension, while activated endothelium leaks fluid and expresses tissue factor, which starts consumptive coagulation (DIC). Poor perfusion forces anaerobic metabolism, producing lactic acidosis and organ failure. Superantigens skip antigen processing by linking class II directly to the TCR V-beta region, so they activate T cells regardless of peptide specificity and cause a similar cytokine storm.

summary: How the three complement pathways start, what complement pieces do, how the body keeps complement in check, and what goes wrong when a part is missing. Exams lean on deficiency patterns and on reading C3 and C4 levels.

points: Classical: C1q binds the Fc of IgM (one bound pentamer is enough) or of two or more bound IgG molecules; C1r and C1s then cut C4 and C2.
Lectin: mannose-binding lectin (MBL) binds mannose-rich sugars on microbes; its MASPs cut C4 and C2.
Classical and lectin pathways both make the C3 convertase C4b2a.
Alternative: C3 breaks down slowly on its own (tickover); C3b that lands on a microbe binds factor B, which factor D cuts, making C3bBb, stabilized by properdin.
All three converge on C3 convertase, then C5 convertase, then C5b to C9.
notes.why: All three pathways solve the same problem, placing a C3 convertase on a target surface, but they recognize the target differently. The classical pathway needs bound antibody because C1q must bind two Fc regions close together, which one bound IgM pentamer provides but IgG provides only when several molecules bind near each other. The lectin pathway recognizes microbial sugars directly, and the alternative pathway relies on constant low-level C3 hydrolysis, with C3b surviving and building convertases only on surfaces that lack host regulators. Each C3b made can form more alternative convertase, so the alternative pathway amplifies whichever pathway started the process.

points: C3b: opsonin that coats microbes for phagocytes; also tags immune complexes.
C3a and C5a (and weaker C4a): anaphylatoxins that make mast cells release histamine.
C5a: strong neutrophil chemoattractant.
C5b to C9: membrane attack complex (MAC) that punches holes in thin-walled cells such as Neisseria.
Immune complex clearance: C3b-coated complexes bind CR1 on red cells and are carried to the liver and spleen for removal.
notes.why: Cleaving C3 and C5 splits each into a small soluble fragment and a larger fragment that binds the target. The bound C3b marks microbes for phagocytes and immune complexes for transport, while the soluble C3a and C5a diffuse away and act on mast cells and neutrophils to start inflammation. C5b then begins the membrane attack complex, which matters most clinically against Neisseria, whose thin outer membrane is vulnerable to lysis; most other bacteria are cleared mainly by opsonization.

points: C1 esterase inhibitor blocks C1r, C1s, and MASPs, and also kallikrein and factor XIIa.
DAF (CD55) breaks apart C3 convertases on host cells; CD59 blocks MAC assembly.
Hereditary angioedema: C1 inhibitor deficiency (autosomal dominant) lets kallikrein make excess bradykinin.
It causes nonpitting swelling of face, lips, larynx, or gut, without hives or itching; C4 is low, C3 is normal, and ACE inhibitors are avoided.
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: an acquired PIGA mutation in a stem cell blocks GPI anchors, so CD55 and CD59 are missing.
PNH causes complement-driven intravascular hemolysis, dark morning urine, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis; flow cytometry shows missing CD55 and CD59.
notes.why: Complement is always running at a low level, so host cells need constant protection, and the regulators act at the start (C1 inhibitor), the C3 convertase step (DAF), and the final step (CD59). C1 inhibitor also controls the contact system, so its deficiency raises bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability without mast cell activation, giving deep swelling without hives; ongoing C1 activity also consumes C4. ACE normally breaks down bradykinin, which is why ACE inhibitors worsen this angioedema. In PNH, the PIGA mutation blocks GPI anchor synthesis, so DAF and CD59 cannot attach to red cells, and complement lyses them inside vessels.

points: C1q, C2, or C4 (early classical) deficiency: immune complexes are cleared poorly, causing SLE-like disease.
C3 deficiency: severe recurrent pyogenic infections (encapsulated bacteria) and immune complex glomerulonephritis.
C5 to C9 (terminal) deficiency: recurrent Neisseria infections, especially meningococcal disease.
MBL deficiency: more infections in infancy and early childhood, usually mild.
Eculizumab (anti-C5) used for PNH creates the same Neisseria risk, so patients receive meningococcal vaccine.
notes.why: The clinical pattern follows the function lost. Early classical components help clear immune complexes and apoptotic debris, so their loss lets nuclear antigens linger and drive SLE-like autoimmunity. C3 sits at the center of opsonization, so its loss impairs clearance of both encapsulated bacteria and immune complexes. Terminal components matter mainly for lysing Neisseria, so their loss causes recurrent meningococcal and gonococcal infection, and blocking C5 with eculizumab creates the same risk. MBL deficiency shows up mostly in the window after maternal antibody fades and before the child's own antibody responses mature.

points: Low C3 and low C4: classical pathway consumption by immune complexes, as in active SLE.
Low C3 with normal C4: alternative pathway consumption, as in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis; C3 usually recovers within about 8 weeks.
Low C4 with normal C3: C1 inhibitor deficiency in hereditary angioedema.
Falling C3 and C4 in a lupus patient suggest a flare.
notes.why: Serum levels fall when consumption outpaces liver synthesis, and the active pathway decides which component falls. Classical activation by immune complexes cleaves C4 and C2 before C3, so both C4 and C3 drop, while alternative pathway activation cleaves C3 without using C4. In hereditary angioedema, unchecked C1s keeps cleaving C4 but generates little C3 convertase, so C4 is low while C3 stays normal. Serial levels therefore track disease activity, such as falling C3 and C4 warning of a lupus flare.

tricks.label: Need two IgG, one IgM
tricks.text: C1q must grab two Fc regions side by side. One IgM pentamer offers several at once; IgG needs at least two molecules close together.

tricks.label: C5 to C9 means Neisseria
tricks.text: The MAC is how the body kills Neisseria. Anyone without a working MAC, by gene defect or by eculizumab, is at risk of meningococcal disease.

tricks.label: Swelling with no itch
tricks.text: Hives and itching point to histamine. Deep swelling without hives that does not respond to antihistamines points to bradykinin and C1 inhibitor deficiency.

highYield: Recurrent meningococcal infection means a terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency until proven otherwise.
Early classical component deficiency (C1q, C2, C4) predisposes to SLE.
Hereditary angioedema: low C4, normal C3, no hives, and ACE inhibitors are contraindicated.
PNH: missing CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry, intravascular hemolysis, and thrombosis in unusual sites such as the hepatic veins.
C5a is the complement fragment that recruits neutrophils.
Low C3 with normal C4 after a strep throat or skin infection points to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
pitfalls: C3b is the main opsonin; C3a is an anaphylatoxin. For C3 and C5, the b fragment stays on the surface and the a fragment floats away.
Angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency is bradykinin driven; allergic angioedema is histamine driven and comes with hives.
Early component deficiency causes autoimmunity; terminal component deficiency causes Neisseria infections.
PNH is an acquired stem cell mutation, not an inherited complement deficiency.

flows.title: Classical pathway
steps: IgM or clustered IgG binds antigen on a target surface
C1q binds the antibody Fc regions, activating C1r and then C1s
C1s cleaves C4 and C2, forming the C3 convertase C4b2a
C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b
C3b joins to form C5 convertase, which cleaves C5
C5b recruits C6 to C9 to form the membrane attack complex

flows.title: Alternative pathway
steps: Spontaneous C3 hydrolysis (tickover) generates small amounts of C3b
C3b binds a microbial surface that lacks host regulators
Factor B binds C3b, and factor D cleaves it, forming C3bBb
Properdin stabilizes C3bBb, which cleaves more C3 and amplifies deposition
Added C3b forms C5 convertase, which cleaves C5
C5b recruits C6 to C9 to form the membrane attack complex

flows.title: Hereditary angioedema
steps: C1 esterase inhibitor is deficient (autosomal dominant)
Kallikrein and factor XIIa activity go unchecked
Kallikrein cleaves high molecular weight kininogen, releasing bradykinin
Bradykinin increases vascular permeability
Nonpitting swelling of face, larynx, or gut occurs without hives
